title: Bengaluru Deploys AI-Powered Dashcam System to Map and Fix Potholes Citywide
excerpt: The Bengaluru East City Corporation is using YOLO-based computer vision to scan 1,600 km of roads, while a local startup has built a real-time pothole detector trained on 47,000 images from Indian cities.
body:
• Bengaluru East City Corporation (BECC) has deployed AI-equipped survey vehicles across all 50 wards, scanning 1,600 km of roads and assigning each a unique Road Identification Number.
  • The system uses YOLO (You Only Look Once) computer vision to detect potholes, cracks, and road damage, categorizing every segment into five condition levels.
  • A Bengaluru startup called Anomaly has independently built a real-time dashcam-based pothole detector trained on nearly 47,000 images from cities including Delhi, Pune, Mumbai, and Jaipur.
  • In a pilot at Vibhuthipura, the BECC system identified 144 potholes across the ward — roughly 17 per kilometre — with officials ordering repairs within one week.

From Manual Inspections to AI Scanning

Bengaluru's pothole problem has been a perennial headache for its residents, with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways reporting thousands of road accident deaths linked to potholes across India each year. Now, the city is turning to artificial intelligence to move from reactive repair to data-driven road maintenance.

https://x.com/NDTVProfit/status/2088992316665245874

The Bengaluru East City Corporation (BECC) has launched an AI-powered road monitoring initiative that replaces manual inspections with computer vision. Survey vehicles fitted with high-resolution cameras have scanned nearly 1,600 km of roads across the BECC region. The footage is analyzed using YOLO (You Only Look Once), an AI-based object detection model that identifies potholes, cracks, rutting, and utility cuts in real time.

Every road segment is assigned one of five condition categories, giving engineers a consistent picture of road quality. Each road also receives a unique Road Identification Number, with GPS coordinates, photographs, damage reports, and road details stored in a centralized digital database.

AI Estimates Dimensions for Budget Planning

The system goes beyond simple detection. A Vision Language Model — which combines image recognition with text analysis — works alongside image segmentation to estimate each pothole's length and width. This helps engineers calculate the hot mix asphalt required for repairs, making budgeting more precise before fieldwork begins.

Depth measurement, however, remains a limitation. Camera-based surveys cannot reliably capture depth, which still requires physical field verification. Despite this constraint, the system provides a substantial improvement over the scattered field reports that previously drove repair prioritization.

Vibhuthipura Pilot Shows Results

The first phase of the survey covered roads across all 50 wards under BECC. Vibhuthipura was selected as the first repair pilot, where the AI system identified approximately 144 potholes and about 144 square metres of patching work — an average of 17 potholes per kilometre.

For every defect, the dashboard records GPS coordinates, estimated dimensions, and photographic evidence. Officials have directed field teams to make Vibhuthipura pothole-free within one week. If the pilot succeeds, BECC plans to extend the system across more wards and run seasonal surveys before and after the monsoon.

Startup Builds Crowdsourced Pothole Dataset

Independently of the civic initiative, a Bengaluru-based company called Anomaly has developed its own AI pothole detection system. Led by Virendra Suryawanshi, the system uses the same YOLO framework but is designed for real-time dashcam use — detecting and logging potholes while a vehicle moves through traffic.

"When cities have precise data on pothole locations and severity, repairs can be prioritised and executed more efficiently."

— Virendra Suryawanshi, Anomaly

Anomaly's model has been trained on nearly 47,000 pothole images collected from roads across Bengaluru, Delhi, Aizawl, Jaipur, Pune, Mumbai, Bhopal, Yavatmal, and Gurugram. The team is building what it aims to make India's largest pothole dataset, with contributions crowdsourced from drivers across the country.

Suryawanshi has said his team is open to collaborating with civic agencies, offering live pothole maps, severity assessments, and repair verification tools. The project's dual objectives are building the comprehensive dataset and deploying a real-time mapping system for faster, data-driven road repairs.

What This Means for Indian Cities

Bengaluru's approach reflects a broader trend of Indian cities experimenting with AI for urban infrastructure management. The geotagged data reduces repeated site visits, improves transparency in repair budgets, and helps authorities focus on the worst stretches first.

The technology's value will ultimately depend on how consistently AI detections are verified on the ground and whether civic bodies follow through on the repair data. Automated systems can produce false positives, and the gap between detection and action remains the harder problem to solve. But by combining AI with digital mapping, Bengaluru is at least building the infrastructure to identify problems early rather than reacting after roads have already deteriorated.
nri_angle: AI-driven road monitoring in Indian cities could improve safety for diaspora members visiting or driving in India, while demonstrating the kind of civic tech innovation emerging from Bengaluru's startup ecosystem.
